Jabin
jā'bĭn
n. (a dynastic name of the kings of Hazor — the northern coalition Joshua burned, and the oppressor Deborah broke)
From Hebrew Yabin, he understands or he discerns, from bin, to discern. Two kings bear it a century and a half apart, which suggests a throne-name of the house of Hazor rather than a private name.

Biblical Definition

Jabin is the name on the throne of Hazor, “the head of all those kingdoms” in the north, and it belongs to two men. The first hears of Joshua's southern campaign and assembles the great northern confederacy — “when Jabin king of Hazor had heard those things, that he sent to Jobab king of Madon” (Jos 11:1) — a host with horses and chariots “as the sand that is upon the sea shore”, which Joshua routed at the waters of Merom and whose city he burned. The second reigns in a rebuilt Hazor in the days of the judges: “the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, that reigned in Hazor; the captain of whose host was Sisera” (Jdg 4:2). Nine hundred chariots of iron, twenty years of oppression, and then Deborah and Barak and a rainstorm and a river: “So God subdued on that day Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel” (Jdg 4:23). Asaph still names him in prayer generations later (Psa 83:9). The two Jabins together teach what Judges is for — ground once taken can be lost, and an enemy burned to the foundations can rebuild while the covenant people forget.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no article for Jabin; in sacred history it denotes the kings of Hazor, the first overthrown by Joshua and the second by Deborah and Barak.

expand to see more

JABIN, n. King of Hazor, head of the confederacy of northern Canaan destroyed by Joshua at the waters of Merom.

The name signifies one who understands or discerns.

A second Jabin, reigning in Hazor in the days of the judges, oppressed Israel twenty years.

His captain was Sisera, who had nine hundred chariots of iron.

He was subdued by the hand of Deborah and Barak, and his memory is invoked in the eighty-third Psalm.

Key Scripture

Jos 11:1 — "And it came to pass, when Jabin king of Hazor had heard those things, that he sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph,"

Jdg 4:2 — "And the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, that reigned in Hazor; the captain of whose host was Sisera, which dwelt in Harosheth of the Gentiles."

Jdg 4:23 — "So God subdued on that day Jabin the king of Canaan before the children of Israel."

Psa 83:9 — "Do unto them as unto the Midianites; as to Sisera, as to Jabin, at the brook of Kison:"

Modern Corruption

Judges is read as a cycle of political misfortune; the text says the LORD sold them, which makes the oppressor a rod in a Father's hand rather than an accident of geopolitics.

expand to see more

Jdg 4:2 will not permit a merely political reading of Israel's troubles: “the LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin.” The verb is commercial and deliberate. Israel was not overrun because Hazor had better metallurgy; Israel was handed over, by God, for covenant unfaithfulness, exactly as Deu 28 had said in advance. Modern historiography reverses this — the theology is treated as a later interpretive gloss laid over the real causes, which are chariots and trade routes. Scripture treats the chariots as the instrument and the covenant as the cause, and the whole book of Judges is unintelligible on any other reading.

The second Jabin also rebukes a triumphalism that assumes ground once won stays won. Joshua burned Hazor; Judges finds a Jabin reigning in Hazor again. Nothing in the conquest was undone by God; it was undone by a generation “which knew not the LORD, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel” (Jdg 2:10). Reformation in a church, a family, or a nation is held only by teaching — and the enemy is patient enough to rebuild on his own ashes while the covenant people neglect to catechise their children.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Yabin (H2985), Jabin, from bin (H995), to discern; his city Chatsor (H2674), Hazor, an enclosure.

expand to see more

Hebrew Yabin (H2985) — Jabin; probably a dynastic title of the kings of Hazor.

Hebrew bin (H995) — to discern, understand; the root of the name, ironic in a king who could not read the times.

Hebrew Chatsor (H2674) — Hazor, an enclosure or castle; “the head of all those kingdoms” (Jos 11:10).

Hebrew makar (H4376) — to sell; the LORD's own act in Jdg 4:2, judgment by handing over.

Hebrew kana' (H3665) — to subdue, humble; God's act in Jdg 4:23, the reversal of the selling.

Usage

"“Jabin king of Hazor had heard those things” — the northern coalition forming."

"“The LORD sold them into the hand of Jabin” — oppression as covenant discipline."

"“As to Sisera, as to Jabin” — a prayer that recites old deliverances."
